title: Plan the steps from a client brief to a delivered video
scenario: A bike-bell brand orders a 16-second vertical video ad. You plan the chain from the brief to the delivered file, and you decide what each hand-off must do. Use the exhibit. The notes are made up for this case; the vendor lines are copied from the docs.
exhibit:
BRIEF:
  Client: Spoke & Co, bike bells. Deliverable: one 16-second vertical (9:16)
         video ad. Due Friday 12:00.
  Inputs: a confidential PDF brief about an unreleased bell, 6 product photos,
         the logo.
  Chain (ours): brief -> shot list -> hero still -> two 8-second clips ->
         voice-over -> review -> delivery.

NOTES (made up for this case):
  Brief:     Step 1 uploads the PDF to the studio's one shared Claude workspace,
             with the Files API. Freelancers on a rival client's job (Gear Bros)
             hold API keys for the same workspace.
  Stills:    A test run sent 20 OpenAI image requests. All 20 came back OK. The
             project folder has no image files.
  Chat:      The producer's chat assistant can call make_clip(seconds, ...) for
             Veo 3.1. It just called make_clip(seconds=15). The studio's own
             app would run the call.
  Schedule:  Thursday 17:00, 30 still variants go to the Gemini batch API.
             The client call is Friday 09:00.
  Retries:   The video tool already retries 429 and 503 errors by itself. A
             developer adds a second loop around it: "retry up to 5 times".

VENDOR LINES (copied from the docs):
  Anthropic Files API: "Uploaded files are accessible to your entire workspace,
         not scoped to an end user, conversation, or session."
  OpenAI image guide: "The Image API returns base64-encoded image data."
  Google function calling, best practices: "Validate function calls before executing."
  Google Veo docs, clip length: 4, 6 or 8 seconds.
  Google image docs, batch: "You get higher rate limits in exchange for a
         turnaround of up to 24 hours."
  OpenAI rate limits: "If you manage retries in your application, disable SDK
         retries or account for them in those limits so nested retry loops don't
         multiply requests."

questions.prompt: The brief PDF sits in a Claude workspace that rival freelancers have keys for. What is the problem, and what is the fix?

options.text: Nothing. A file is visible only to the end user and the conversation that uploaded it.
options.explanation: Anthropic says the opposite: uploaded files are not scoped to an end user, conversation or session. They are open to the whole workspace.

options.text: Files are open to every key for the workspace. Keep each client's files in a separate workspace.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic says uploaded files are accessible to your entire workspace. So the confidential brief should live in a workspace the rival's freelancers cannot use.

options.text: The upload is deleted after 48 hours, so the freelancers could not reach it for long, and the risk ends by itself.
options.explanation: That is a different vendor's rule. Anthropic says uploaded files persist until you delete them, or until an expiry you set.

options.text: Rename the file with a code name. A key can see only file names, not what is inside a file, so it stays hidden.
options.explanation: A key with access to the workspace can use the files themselves. A code name does not hide the content.

questions.prompt: The test run says OK for all 20 stills, but the folder has no image files. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The vendor keeps each image in its dashboard, and the team must download them from there by hand.
options.explanation: The image comes back in the response itself, as data. It is not parked in a dashboard waiting for a download.

options.text: Requests made in a conversation never return image data to the studio, only a link to the chat window.
options.explanation: The response carries the image data. OpenAI says the Image API returns base64-encoded image data, so a step that saves it to a file has to be built.

options.text: The quality was set to low, and the vendor does not return images made at low quality.
options.explanation: Low quality is a normal setting for quick drafts. It still returns an image, so it does not explain the empty folder.

options.text: The response holds the image as base64 data, not a file. Someone must add a step to save it.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI says the Image API returns base64-encoded image data. Saving the file is a separate step in the chain, and nobody built it.

questions.prompt: The assistant called make_clip(seconds=15), and the Veo 3.1 clip lengths are 4, 6 or 8 seconds. What should the studio's app do?

options.text: Check the call against the allowed lengths before running it. A tool call is only a request.
options.explanation: Right. Google lists "Validate function calls before executing" as a best practice. The model asks, and your app checks the request before it runs.

options.text: Run it as it is. The video tool will cut a 15-second request down to a valid length by itself.
options.explanation: Nothing in the docs says it will fix a wrong value for you. A bad value can fail, or waste a render, if nobody checks.

options.text: Run it as it is. The model knows the tool's limits well, so its values do not need a check.
options.explanation: The model only writes the request. It can be wrong, so the app checks it. This is the reason for validating calls.

options.text: Have a person approve every make_clip call first, the same way as for a tool that posts to social media.
options.explanation: A person belongs before a send tool, such as posting. A make tool only creates a draft, and a wrong call costs a little time. A check in code is enough.

questions.prompt: The 30 still variants go to the Gemini batch API on Thursday at 17:00, and the client call is Friday at 09:00. What do you tell the producer?

options.text: The stills will be ready by 09:00, because 16 hours is less than the 24 hours the vendor lists.
options.explanation: The 24 hours is the longest time a batch can take, not a promise of speed. A batch can still be running at 09:00.

options.text: Batch jobs finish in minutes. Promise the stills for the call, and use the spare hours for review.
options.explanation: Google says a batch has a turnaround of up to 24 hours. It is built for work that can wait, not for minutes.

options.text: A batch can take up to 24 hours, so it may miss the call. Send must-see stills as standard calls.
options.explanation: Right. Batch trades speed for higher rate limits. Work needed at a set time should not wait in a queue that can take a day.

options.text: Check the batch job every second all night. Constant checking makes the job finish sooner.
options.explanation: Checking does not speed up a job. It only adds requests, and constant polling is not how a job should be watched.

questions.prompt: A developer adds a retry loop of 5 tries around a video tool that already retries 429 and 503 errors. What do you flag?

options.text: No risk. More retries only mean more finished clips, so a higher number of tries is always better.
options.explanation: More retries are not always better. Each failure can add requests and cost, and retries are meant to be capped in attempts and in total time.

options.text: Two retry loops multiply requests. Ask what the tool already retries, and cap tries and time.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI warns that nested retry loops multiply requests, and says to limit both the attempts and the total time spent retrying.

options.text: The extra loop is needed, because the vendors' SDKs never retry a 429 or a 503 error by themselves.
options.explanation: OpenAI says its official SDKs automatically retry eligible 429 and 503 responses. A second loop on top of that is why requests multiply.

options.text: The only risk is cost, and failed requests are always free, so the extra loop is safe to add.
options.explanation: Failed requests are not always free. Runway charges the same credits for a moderated request as for a good one, and OpenAI says unsuccessful requests count toward your per-minute limit.
